question: Is it better to be healthy or wealthy?
title: health versus wealth
hook: Does a fat bank account beat a clean bill of health?
answer: In personal happiness, health easily wins: 39% of lowest-income Americans in excellent health report being very happy, compared to just 18% of highest-income Americans in poor health.

stats.label: of lowest-income people in excellent health reporting very happy
of highest-income people in poor health reporting very happy
of country-years where national wealth contributes more than health

followups: Does the health-happiness gap narrow in wealthier nations?
How did pandemic-era survey changes affect reported well-being?
Does the impact of income on happiness level off?
body:
## health beats wealth at home

If you had to trade your physical well-being for a larger paycheck, the data suggests you would be making a poor deal. Self-reported health has a stronger association with happiness than family income (GSS 1972-2024). 

The gap in "very happy" rates between those in excellent and poor health is **30 percentage points** (GSS 1972-2024). By contrast, the gap between the top and bottom income quintiles is only 17 percentage points (GSS 1972-2024).

Having a high income does not seem to compensate for the drag of poor health (GSS 1972-2024). Among high earners in the top income quintile who report poor health, only **18%** say they are very happy (GSS 1972-2024). Meanwhile, among those in the lowest income quintile who report excellent health, 39% report being very happy (GSS 1972-2024).

```chart
{"type": "bar", "title": "Excellent health correlates with happiness more than high income", "y_label": "share saying they are very happy", "unit": "%", "labels": ["Excellent, low income", "Excellent, high income", "Poor, low income", "Poor, high income"], "series": [{"name": "very happy", "data": [39.2, 52.8, 15.9, 17.8]}], "highlight": "Excellent, low income", "note": "Based on GSS respondents in the top and bottom income quintiles."}
```

## national wealth tells a different story

When we look at entire nations rather than individuals, the balance shifts toward the economic side (WHR 2026). Across countries, the estimated contribution of wealth to overall life evaluation is more than twice as large as the contribution of health (WHR 2026).

The average contribution of wealth is **1.3 points** on a 10-point scale, compared to 0.6 points for health (WHR 2026). This contribution is remarkably stable relative to health across all happiness levels (WHR 2026).

National wealth contributes more to life evaluation than health in **96%** of all country-years (WHR 2026). The rare exceptions where health contributes more are almost exclusively countries experiencing severe economic collapse, such as Venezuela (WHR 2026). Both factors, however, remain strongly positively correlated with how people evaluate their lives overall (WHR 2026).

```chart
{"type": "bar", "title": "Wealth consistently contributes more to life evaluations than health", "y_label": "estimated contribution to life evaluation", "unit": "", "labels": ["Unhappiest fifth", "Second fifth", "Middle fifth", "Fourth fifth", "Happiest fifth"], "series": [{"name": "Wealth contribution", "data": [0.8, 1.0, 1.3, 1.5, 1.7]}, {"name": "Health contribution", "data": [0.3, 0.4, 0.6, 0.6, 0.8]}], "note": "Average contribution to the 0-10 life evaluation scale by country-year quintile."}
```

## the physical baseline remains remarkably stable

Over the decades, the gap in happiness between those in excellent and poor health has stayed wide and steady (GSS 1972-2024). In the 1972–1989 period, Americans in excellent health were 2.5 times more likely to report being very happy than those in poor health (GSS 1972-2024).

By the 2010–2018 period, they were **3 times** more likely to say they were very happy (GSS 1972-2024). This gap persisted even as overall reported happiness levels fell across all groups in recent years (GSS 1972-2024).

When you look at the entire timeline, only **7%** of people in excellent health report being not too happy (GSS 1972-2024). For those in poor health, that share rises to 38% (GSS 1972-2024). This pattern holds even when looking within specific income groups (GSS 1972-2024).

```chart
{"type": "bar", "title": "Unhappiness rises dramatically as self-reported health declines", "y_label": "share of respondents", "unit": "%", "labels": ["Excellent health", "Good health", "Fair health", "Poor health"], "series": [{"name": "very happy", "data": [46.4, 27.9, 19.1, 16.5]}, {"name": "not too happy", "data": [7.2, 11.6, 23.3, 37.8]}], "note": "Weighted shares of GSS respondents from 1972 to 2024."}
```

## what this data can't tell you

First, we cannot know if the sharp drop in happiness after 2020 reflects real societal changes or simply the survey's shift from in-person interviews to web forms. Second, the income groups are estimates based on pre-set brackets, which means some household incomes are split across different groups. Finally, the national-level contributions are statistical estimates measured against a hypothetical worst-case country, not direct, simple measures of GDP or life expectancy.

trail.task: In the GSS dataset, how does self-reported health (health/health_label) relate to happiness (happy/happy_label)? What is the weighted percentage of 'very happy' (happy = 1) respondents across the different health levels (excellent, good, fair, poor), excluding NULLs?

queries.sql: SELECT health, health_label, COUNT(*), SUM(weight) FROM gss WHERE health IS NOT NULL GROUP BY 1, 2 ORDER BY health;
SELECT happy, happy_label, COUNT(*), SUM(weight) FROM gss WHERE happy IS NOT NULL GROUP BY 1, 2 ORDER BY happy;

SELECT
  health,
  health_label,
  SUM(weight * (happy = 1)::INT) / SUM(weight) AS pct_very_happy,
  SUM(weight * (happy = 2)::INT) / SUM(weight) AS pct_pretty_happy,
  SUM(weight * (happy = 3)::INT) / SUM(weight) AS pct_not_too_happy,
  SUM(weight) AS total_weight,
  COUNT(*) AS raw_count
FROM gss
WHERE health IS NOT NULL AND happy IS NOT NULL
GROUP BY health, health_label
ORDER BY health;

SELECT
  CASE
    WHEN year < 1990 THEN '1972-1989'
    WHEN year < 2010 THEN '1990-2009'
    WHEN year < 2020 THEN '2010-2018'
    ELSE '2021-2024 (web/mixed)'
  END AS time_period,
  health_label,
  SUM(weight * (happy = 1)::INT) / SUM(weight) AS pct_very_happy,
  SUM(weight) AS total_weight,
  COUNT(*) AS raw_count
FROM gss
WHERE health IS NOT NULL AND happy IS NOT NULL
GROUP BY 1, health, health_label
ORDER BY 1, health;
SELECT COUNT(*), COUNT(family_income_2024usd) FROM gss WHERE health IS NOT NULL AND happy IS NOT NULL;

WITH ranked_gss AS (
  SELECT
    health_label,
    health,
    happy,
    weight,
    NTILE(3) OVER (ORDER BY family_income_2024usd) AS income_tertile
  FROM gss
  WHERE health IS NOT NULL AND happy IS NOT NULL AND family_income_2024usd IS NOT NULL
)
SELECT
  income_tertile,
  health_label,
  SUM(weight * (happy = 1)::INT) / SUM(weight) AS pct_very_happy,
  SUM(weight) AS total_weight,
  COUNT(*) AS raw_count
FROM ranked_gss
GROUP BY income_tertile, health, health_label
ORDER BY income_tertile, health;

trail.task: In the GSS dataset, how does family income relate to happiness? What is the weighted percentage of 'very happy' (happy = 1) respondents across quintiles of family_income_2024usd, excluding NULLs?

queries.sql: SELECT MIN(family_income_2024usd), MAX(family_income_2024usd), COUNT(*), COUNT(family_income_2024usd) FROM gss;
SELECT happy, happy_label, COUNT(*), SUM(weight) FROM gss GROUP BY happy, happy_label;
SELECT COUNT(*) FROM gss WHERE family_income_2024usd IS NOT NULL AND happy IS NOT NULL;

WITH ranked AS (
  SELECT
    happy,
    weight,
    family_income_2024usd,
    NTILE(5) OVER (ORDER BY family_income_2024usd) as quintile
  FROM gss
  WHERE family_income_2024usd IS NOT NULL AND happy IS NOT NULL
)
SELECT
  quintile,
  MIN(family_income_2024usd) as min_income,
  MAX(family_income_2024usd) as max_income,
  COUNT(*) as raw_count,
  SUM(weight) as weighted_count,
  SUM(weight * (happy = 1)::INT) / SUM(weight) as pct_very_happy,
  SUM(weight * (happy = 2)::INT) / SUM(weight) as pct_pretty_happy,
  SUM(weight * (happy = 3)::INT) / SUM(weight) as pct_not_too_happy
FROM ranked
GROUP BY quintile
ORDER BY quintile;

WITH ranked AS (
  SELECT
    year,
    happy,
    weight,
    family_income_2024usd,
    NTILE(5) OVER (ORDER BY family_income_2024usd) as quintile
  FROM gss
  WHERE family_income_2024usd IS NOT NULL AND happy IS NOT NULL
),
eras AS (
  SELECT
    *,
    CASE
      WHEN year < 2000 THEN '1972-1999'
      WHEN year BETWEEN 2000 AND 2018 THEN '2000-2018'
      ELSE '2021-2024 (Web/Mixed)'
    END as era
  FROM ranked
)
SELECT
  era,
  quintile,
  MIN(family_income_2024usd) as min_income,
  MAX(family_income_2024usd) as max_income,
  SUM(weight * (happy = 1)::INT) / SUM(weight) as pct_very_happy
FROM eras
GROUP BY era, quintile
ORDER BY era, quintile;

WITH eras AS (
  SELECT
    year,
    happy,
    weight,
    family_income_2024usd,
    CASE
      WHEN year < 2000 THEN '1972-1999'
      WHEN year BETWEEN 2000 AND 2018 THEN '2000-2018'
      ELSE '2021-2024 (Web/Mixed)'
    END as era
  FROM gss
  WHERE family_income_2024usd IS NOT NULL AND happy IS NOT NULL
),
ranked_within_era AS (
  SELECT
    *,
    NTILE(5) OVER (PARTITION BY era ORDER BY family_income_2024usd) as quintile
  FROM eras
)
SELECT
  era,
  quintile,
  MIN(family_income_2024usd) as min_income,
  MAX(family_income_2024usd) as max_income,
  COUNT(*) as raw_count,
  SUM(weight * (happy = 1)::INT) / SUM(weight) as pct_very_happy
FROM ranked_within_era
GROUP BY era, quintile
ORDER BY era, quintile;

trail.task: In the GSS dataset, if we look at both health and family income quintiles together, which one has a stronger association with happiness? For instance, what is the weighted percentage of 'very happy' (happy = 1) for someone in excellent health but the bottom income quintile, versus someone in poor health but the top income quintile?

queries.sql:
SELECT health, health_label, COUNT(*), MIN(year), MAX(year)
FROM gss
WHERE health IS NOT NULL
GROUP BY health, health_label
ORDER BY health;
SELECT COUNT(DISTINCT family_income_2024usd) FROM gss WHERE family_income_2024usd IS NOT NULL;

WITH ordered AS (
  SELECT
    family_income_2024usd,
    weight,
    SUM(weight) OVER (ORDER BY family_income_2024usd) as cum_weight,
    SUM(weight) OVER () as total_weight
  FROM gss
  WHERE family_income_2024usd IS NOT NULL AND health IS NOT NULL AND happy IS NOT NULL
)
SELECT
  MIN(family_income_2024usd) as min_inc,
  MAX(family_income_2024usd) as max_inc,
  SUM(weight) as total_w,
  CASE
    WHEN cum_weight <= total_weight * 0.2 THEN 1
    WHEN cum_weight <= total_weight * 0.4 THEN 2
    WHEN cum_weight <= total_weight * 0.6 THEN 3
    WHEN cum_weight <= total_weight * 0.8 THEN 4
    ELSE 5
  END as quintile
FROM ordered
GROUP BY quintile
ORDER BY quintile;

WITH ordered AS (
  SELECT
    id,
    year,
    health,
    health_label,
    family_income_2024usd,
    happy,
    weight,
    SUM(weight) OVER (ORDER BY family_income_2024usd) as cum_weight,
    SUM(weight) OVER () as total_weight
  FROM gss
  WHERE family_income_2024usd IS NOT NULL AND health IS NOT NULL AND happy IS NOT NULL
),
categorized AS (
  SELECT
    id,
    year,
    health,
    health_label,
    happy,
    weight,
    CASE
      WHEN cum_weight <= total_weight * 0.2 THEN 1
      WHEN cum_weight <= total_weight * 0.4 THEN 2
      WHEN cum_weight <= total_weight * 0.6 THEN 3
      WHEN cum_weight <= total_weight * 0.8 THEN 4
      ELSE 5
    END as quintile
  FROM ordered
)
SELECT
  health,
  health_label,
  quintile,
  SUM(weight) as sample_weight,
  COUNT(*) as raw_count,
  SUM(weight * (happy = 1)::INT) / SUM(weight) * 100 as pct_very_happy,
  SUM(weight * (happy = 3)::INT) / SUM(weight) * 100 as pct_not_too_happy
FROM categorized
GROUP BY health, health_label, quintile
ORDER BY health, quintile;

WITH ordered AS (
  SELECT
    health,
    family_income_2024usd,
    happy,
    weight,
    SUM(weight) OVER (ORDER BY family_income_2024usd) as cum_weight,
    SUM(weight) OVER () as total_weight
  FROM gss
  WHERE family_income_2024usd IS NOT NULL AND health IS NOT NULL AND happy IS NOT NULL
),
categorized AS (
  SELECT
    health,
    happy,
    weight,
    CASE
      WHEN cum_weight <= total_weight * 0.2 THEN 1
      WHEN cum_weight <= total_weight * 0.4 THEN 2
      WHEN cum_weight <= total_weight * 0.6 THEN 3
      WHEN cum_weight <= total_weight * 0.8 THEN 4
      ELSE 5
    END as quintile
  FROM ordered
)
SELECT 'Health' as dimension, CAST(health as VARCHAR) as category, SUM(weight * (happy = 1)::INT) / SUM(weight) * 100 as pct_very_happy, SUM(weight) as sample_w
FROM categorized
GROUP BY health
UNION ALL
SELECT 'Income Quintile' as dimension, CAST(quintile as VARCHAR) as category, SUM(weight * (happy = 1)::INT) / SUM(weight) * 100 as pct_very_happy, SUM(weight) as sample_w
FROM categorized
GROUP BY quintile
ORDER BY dimension, category;

trail.task: In the WHR (World Happiness Report) dataset, how do the contributions of wealth (explained_by_gdp_per_capita) and health (explained_by_healthy_life_expectancy) to life evaluation compare? What are their average values, and how do they correlate with life_evaluation?

queries.sql:
SELECT
    COUNT(*) AS total_rows,
    COUNT(explained_by_gdp_per_capita) AS non_null_gdp,
    MIN(year) AS min_year,
    MAX(year) AS max_year
FROM whr

SELECT
    AVG(life_evaluation) AS avg_life_evaluation,
    AVG(explained_by_gdp_per_capita) AS avg_gdp,
    AVG(explained_by_healthy_life_expectancy) AS avg_health,
    CORR(explained_by_gdp_per_capita, life_evaluation) AS corr_gdp_life,
    CORR(explained_by_healthy_life_expectancy, life_evaluation) AS corr_health_life,
    CORR(explained_by_gdp_per_capita, explained_by_healthy_life_expectancy) AS corr_gdp_health,
    MIN(explained_by_gdp_per_capita) AS min_gdp,
    MAX(explained_by_gdp_per_capita) AS max_gdp,
    MIN(explained_by_healthy_life_expectancy) AS min_health,
    MAX(explained_by_healthy_life_expectancy) AS max_health
FROM whr
WHERE explained_by_gdp_per_capita IS NOT NULL

queries.sql:
SELECT
    year,
    COUNT(*) AS count,
    AVG(life_evaluation) AS avg_life,
    AVG(explained_by_gdp_per_capita) AS avg_gdp,
    AVG(explained_by_healthy_life_expectancy) AS avg_health,
    CORR(explained_by_gdp_per_capita, life_evaluation) AS corr_gdp_life,
    CORR(explained_by_healthy_life_expectancy, life_evaluation) AS corr_health_life
FROM whr
WHERE explained_by_gdp_per_capita IS NOT NULL
GROUP BY year
ORDER BY year

SELECT
    COUNT(*) AS total_country_years,
    SUM(CASE WHEN explained_by_healthy_life_expectancy > explained_by_gdp_per_capita THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS health_gt_gdp,
    SUM(CASE WHEN explained_by_gdp_per_capita > explained_by_healthy_life_expectancy THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS gdp_gt_health
FROM whr
WHERE explained_by_gdp_per_capita IS NOT NULL

SELECT
    country,
    year,
    life_evaluation,
    explained_by_gdp_per_capita AS gdp,
    explained_by_healthy_life_expectancy AS health
FROM whr
WHERE explained_by_healthy_life_expectancy > explained_by_gdp_per_capita
ORDER BY (health - gdp) DESC
LIMIT 20

WITH binned AS (
    SELECT
        NTILE(5) OVER (ORDER BY life_evaluation) AS happiness_quintile,
        life_evaluation,
        explained_by_gdp_per_capita AS gdp,
        explained_by_healthy_life_expectancy AS health
    FROM whr
    WHERE explained_by_gdp_per_capita IS NOT NULL
)
SELECT
    happiness_quintile,
    ROUND(AVG(life_evaluation), 2) AS avg_life,
    ROUND(AVG(gdp), 3) AS avg_gdp,
    ROUND(AVG(health), 3) AS avg_health,
    ROUND(AVG(gdp) / AVG(health), 2) AS gdp_to_health_ratio,
    COUNT(*) AS count
FROM binned
GROUP BY happiness_quintile
ORDER BY happiness_quintile
